glossary.meaning: Conscience is the inner court where our whole teaching plays out. Under God's Law, it feels terror. Under God's promise, it finds comfort. It is not a guide that tells us right from wrong. It is a court that stands accused, then is set free.
glossary.world_word: conscience -- 'terrified,' 'anxious,' 'captive'; the court where our doctrine is decided

glossary.meaning: Faith is trust that holds onto God's own promise. It is not simply believing a story is true. This trust alone makes us right with God, apart from our works. But faith never stands on nothing. It rests on the Word and the sacraments.
glossary.world_word: faith -- trust that clings to God's promise, 'faith alone'

glossary.meaning: The household is where our catechism is taught. A father questions his family and servants every week. He leads prayer three times a day. This is how ordinary people learn the faith.
glossary.world_word: the household -- father, wife, children, servants; the catechism's own site

glossary.meaning: God rules us two ways. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom, and makes us Christians. Through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom, and restrains evil. We keep both, and confuse neither with the other.
glossary.world_word: the two governments -- God's spiritual rule by the Word, and secular rule by the sword

glossary.meaning: Baptism makes every one of us a priest. There is no rank among us, only different tasks. A father is a priest in his own home. Still, no one may preach in public without being properly called.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the Small Catechism's Second Article -- the creed and its explanation, said by the household itself, in its own first person, as 'I believe'
pull_quotes.text:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the Augsburg Confession, Article VII -- signed at the 1530 Diet of Augsburg by the electors, princes, and free cities who confessed it, not one preacher's own private teaching
pull_quotes.text:
We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly.
For the true unity of the Church, it is enough to agree on the teaching of the good news and on how the sacraments are given. Nor is it necessary for human traditions -- that is, rites or ceremonies set up by people -- to be alike everywhere. As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the Large Catechism, the Seventh Commandment's own household explanation
pull_quotes.text: But be careful of this. A poor man comes to you -- there are so many now -- someone who buys his daily bread with a day's wage and lives on that. Say you treat him harshly. Say you act as though everyone lived only by your favor. Say you squeeze him to the bone, then turn him away with pride, when you owed him help for nothing. He will go away wretched and sorrowful. He has no one else to complain to, so he will cry out to heaven. Be careful of that, I say again, the way you would be careful of the devil himself. That cry is no small thing. It carries a weight too heavy for you, and for the whole world besides. It reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful. He will not let it go unanswered.

The sinner is 'freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith' (AC IV, 234-239). Works and merit are refused as the ground: 'faith alone, without works, justifies, makes free and saves' (Treatise on Christian Liberty, v2 11780-11781); 'the promises of God give what the commands of God ask... He alone commands. He also alone fulfils' (v2 11817-11820).
Its first, limited form is the target of the 1517 disputation: 'The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and the grace of God' (Th. 62). That thesis answers the claim that giving to the poor is 'a better work than buying pardons' (Th. 43).
The doctrine runs through seven streams of evidence, in both of this world's voices: disputation, treatise, sermon, catechism teaching, and hymn, along with the sustained argument of The Bondage of the Will and Melanchthon's confession. That confession calls it 'the chief topic of Christian doctrine' (Ap IV, 561-562).
It recurs across all seven streams, and other gravities say in their own texts that they depend on it. Promise and sign approaches the sacrament "with faith alone," and the terrified and comforted conscience refers the whole doctrine to the conscience (AC 552-553). Estate, office, and calling redefines works by faith, while vows, chastity, and marriage refuses vows as merit.
It shapes people as a doctrine prescribed and preached, and it is the one gravity the founder says his own congregation already held, in 1522: 'you are more learned herein than I' (v2 14665-14666). That any wider congregation held it rests only on thin inference, so what the founder prescribed is kept apart from what congregations received.
Much of the movement's shape follows from it, including the target of the 1517 protest and the structure of the 1520 treatises. It also explains why the catechism puts the Creed over the Commandments, and why the Confession's own order sets Article IV before Article V.
It persists from 1517 to 1531 in every kind of writing, but by the 1540s it thins to hymn and Table Talk only.
It reinforces the Word, promise and sign, and the household catechism, as well as the conscience, "must" and "free", vows and marriage, and embattled Christendom. Its reinforcement of the bodily presence and German for the people is only thin. It reshapes the two governments and estate, office, and calling, and it competes with only one: hearers and repeaters of words.
The doctrine is well documented, and within this world's own writings the case for it is strong on every count. The confession's own voice calls it "the chief topic," and the evidence fully bears that organizing weight rather than falling short of it.
It appears in both of this world's voices, across six kinds of writing. There is also one thin trace from a household: Katharina von Bora (TT 3147-3148), who speaks of coldness in prayer, not of faith itself. As for how it was received, the founder says it was received, in Wittenberg only, in 1522.
It arose from the friar's founding conviction and from the laity's need for assurance. The papal bull and the Leipzig dispute then turned an argument into the movement's identity, and that papal pressure, in its early and its ongoing form, held and intensified it.
The imperial force intensified it again into a confessional definition at Augsburg: Article IV of the Augsburg Confession in 1530, and the Apology's "chief topic" in 1531.
Then the reform's own "new spirits", the internal radical force, used the formula for a purpose it was not built for. The doctrine was fenced again rather than broken, and by 1529 the Large Catechism answers that faith 'must have something which it believes... upon which it stands and rests' (LC 3916-3921).
After 1531 it is carried only in hymn and Table Talk, a stage that lies at the edge of the world's time window, outside the formal forces mapping.

In the confessional voice's own doctrine of justification, "accounted righteous" (imputed, forensic) names the term's real and controlling sense, and "the making of a righteous man out of an unrighteous" is the same single act described a second, looser way - not an independent claim standing beside the first, but a paraphrase of it, subordinate to it.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Did you believe people are saved by faith alone, not works?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Yes, and we would ask you to hear what we mean by both words before you judge the claim. Faith, for us, is not simply believing a story is true. It is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside us - conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort - and it never stands on nothing: it rests on the Word and the sacraments. This trust alone is what our confession, signed before the emperor, calls the reason a sinner is freely reckoned right with God, for Christ's sake - not by our own strength, merit, or work. But we do not stop there, because we were accused, in our own time, of teaching that works do not matter, and we answer that accusation directly: it is necessary to do good works, not to earn grace by them, but because God commands them. Good works, for us, are not only prayer, fasting, and almsgiving - that names them too narrowly. They are the ordinary things a person does in faith: working, walking, eating, sleeping, none of it good without faith, all of it good in faith, commanded and never a price. Our own confession even states this two ways in one paragraph - that a person is reckoned righteous, and that a person is made righteous out of an unrighteous one - and does not itself say which wording rules the other; we do not settle that for you either. What we hold firmly is this: nothing a person does buys a promise that was always spoken first.

The three parts every Christian must know are to be taught by the father, examined weekly, and sung and prayed morning and evening. 'the ordinary Christian, who cannot read the Scriptures, is required to learn and know the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer... these three contain fully and completely everything that is in the Scriptures' (v2 13182-13186). 'it is the duty of every father of a family to question and examine his children and servants at least once a week' (LC 241-243). 'The Simple Way a Father Should Present Them to His Household' (SC 45).
This gravity is deliberately limited: it is a claim about the program, and it never claims that any household actually held to it.
The program recurs widely, appearing in catechism teaching, in sermons by implication, in a hymnal preface, and in conversation. It also appears in the confession and the Apology and in one participant's witness, and other gravities depend on it broadly.
Its shaping power splits in two, and that split is the central tension in how this gravity is judged. As a prescribed program it holds fully. It is the most fully specified way of forming people in the whole library, reaching down to reciting at mealtimes and to food withheld until the lessons are repeated (LC 333-336). As formation actually achieved, it rests only on thin inference, because no visitation record, parish register, or lay witness confirms that any household did it.
Its explanatory reach is broad, and it persists across kinds of writing from 1520 to 1543. Across regions, though, it fails, since nothing shows any household or parish outside Wittenberg, so its persistence holds only in part.
It reinforces nearly every other gravity: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, and the terrified and comforted conscience. It also reinforces the two governments; estate, office, and calling; vows, chastity, and marriage; German for the people; and embattled Christendom. Its support for the bodily presence is only thin. It reshapes "must" and "free", and it competes with only one: hearers and repeaters of words.
The written prescriptions are well documented, and Walter's witness is widely accepted. Any household's actual practice rests only on thin inference. Scholars contest how reception should even be read, in the debate that follows Strauss.
This record covers the program as defined above, where the evidence is well attested: the bulk of the 1529 writings, plus the two confessional texts. Read more broadly, to include reception as well as the program, the evidence would place it lower. This record states that alternative openly rather than hiding it.
This is the highest-stakes case in this world where how strongly a pattern organizes it and how well that is evidenced pull apart. As a program, it organizes at the highest level this account recognizes, and the program is well attested, but the evidence for how it was received is thin. That thinness is not smoothed over; it is named as sitting outside what this record actually claims.
The program appears in all four kinds of writing and voice, but the mechanism of the father in the household is Luther's alone. Evidence of how it was received is absent, the largest single gap of this kind in this world.
It arose in response to a question: what would replace indulgence, confession, and sacrament as the way lay people were formed? That question itself arose from the laity's need for assurance. Between 1520 and 1529 its audience shifted from "the ordinary Christian, who cannot read" to the negligent pastor and the father of the household. That shift came from the territorial church's own need to inspect.
The state of the parishes, as the founder reported it, intensified it. By its own account, the Large Catechism preface exists because pastors are negligent. Because it is the printed object in the household, print as a medium carried it. It was held within the confessional writings and entered the Book of Concord in 1580 by reference. That links it to the confessional-territorial change and to transmission at the edge of the window. It also carries the household's own daily prayer for the prince, which ties it to the imperial frame.

No single household's own record survives in this library - no diary, no visitation report, no letter from inside a Saxon home. What survives is the program every household was instructed to follow, laid out in careful and repeated detail across the two catechisms, and it is possible to describe that program without inventing anything beyond what it actually says.
A father was to teach the Ten Commandments to his household in what the Small Catechism itself calls "the simple way" - plainly, one at a time, expecting them learned by heart. Mornings began with the sign of the cross and a short prayer asking that "the evil enemy will not gain power over me," and the instruction adds that afterward one might "go about your work and perhaps sing a song inspired by the Ten Commandments." Servants and children were given their own words to use in confession - a servant taught to say plainly that he had "served my master unfaithfully," had at times "not done what I was told to do"; a master or mistress of the house taught, in turn, to confess having "not faithfully led my children, servants or wife to God's glory."
The Large Catechism's own preface makes the weekly rhythm explicit and does not soften its own demand: "it is the duty of every father of a family to question and examine his children and servants at least once a week and to ascertain what they know of it, or are learning and, if they do not know it, to keep them faithfully at it." The same preface states the consequence in plain terms: the household's youngest were to learn the essential parts "word for word" and recite them daily, morning, at meals, and at night, "and until they repeat them, they should be given neither food nor drink." Every head of a household, the preface adds, was bound to hold servants to the same standard, "and not to keep them in his house if they do not know these things and are unwilling to learn them." A Home Chart, appended to the Small Catechism, laid out Scripture texts for every station in the household in turn - pastors, hearers, husbands, wives, parents, children, servants, masters - each given their own duties to be taught and held to.
This is what the library can say: this was the program, stated repeatedly, in the founder's own strongest and most demanding language. Whether any actual household, anywhere in Saxony, carried it out exactly this way, week after week, this library does not say.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: How did a person actually become one of you? Walk me through it.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: A person becomes one of us the way a child becomes one of us: examined, not simply told. Every household is to teach its own the three parts - the commandments first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask. Mornings begin with a short prayer against the enemy. A father questions his children and servants at least once a week on what they know, and asks the catechism's own question after every part - what does this mean - so a truth is explained, not merely repeated back. Confession has two parts too: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself, without doubting it - treasured among us, never compelled and never demanding a full list of every sin. None of this is owed to a person, or earned by them; it is the promise, carried to the ears where it can be heard. We can tell you the whole shape of that program, to the hour. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually walked through it exactly this way - no diary, no visitation report, no letter from inside an actual Saxon home survives in our record. What survives is the program every household was instructed to follow, and it is that program, not any single person's own path through it, that we have just walked you through.

Among the sayings his students recorded at Luther's own table is one about patience. "I must have patience with the Pope," Luther told them; "I must have patience with heretics and seducers; I must have patience with the roaring courtiers; I must have patience with my servants: I must have patience with Kate my wife; to conclude, the patiences are so many, that my whole life is nothing but patience."
In another remembered conversation, Luther told of a time his wife had been sick, and how he had prayed for her recovery - a prayer he believed God had answered, giving the household besides a good farm and a fruitful year. It was around that same telling that Katharina herself is remembered asking him a question: "Sir! how is it, that in Popedom they pray so often with great vehemence, but we are very cold and careless in praying?" Luther's answer, as his students recorded it, was that the devil drives on his own servants continually, diligent in their false worship, "but we, indeed, are ice cold therein, and negligent."
This is the only place in this whole library where Katharina von Bora's own words are recorded at all - one question, remembered by a student, set down years after it was asked, filtered again through later editors before it reached this library. It is not a portrait of her; it is a single sentence.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What was life like for the women among you — in their own words, where your record has them?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: One sentence. That is the whole of what we hold in a woman's own words, anywhere in our record. It was asked at our founder's own table, remembered years later by a student who set it down: why, she wanted to know, did the old church pray so often and with such vehemence, while our own household prayed cold and careless? Her name was Katharina von Bora, our founder's own wife - and that question, passed through several hands before it reached us, is the one place in this whole record where a woman speaks in her own voice at all. Beyond it: nothing. No letter of her own, no second conversation, nothing about her own daily life, her own convictions, or her own formation survives anywhere we hold. We will not build more around that one sentence than it can bear. If you want the women among us in their own words, this is the whole of what our record has to give you - one question, about coldness in prayer, asked once, remembered by someone else.

quiet.statement:
Where is our own record thinnest? On what any actual household or parish did with what it was given. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do -- morning, table, and night. We can tell you exactly what a father was to ask his children and servants each week. That program is the most fully specified thing we hold, down to the hour. Whether it was kept is a different matter. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. What we hold instead is our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real. It is his own, said plainly and said more than once. But it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish. We do not let it stand as one.
Two other places are just as thin. Our fellowship broke plainly with the cities who read the Supper differently. We can state our own position: Christ is truly present, in and under the bread and wine. But the argument itself, and what it felt like from our own side, has not come down to us. The cities' own names barely appear in what we hold at all. And no woman among us left her own word. There is one question, about coldness in prayer, asked at our founder's own table -- but even that was remembered by someone else, not written by her.
That is where we are thinnest. Not on what we were told to believe and do. On what was actually made of it, by real people, past our founder's own testimony about them.

who_speaks.text: Six figures anchor this world's voice, each only as far as the record reaches. Luther began the reform in 1517 and is held in his own letters, sermons, and catechisms. Melanchthon drafted the Augsburg Confession of 1530. Katharina von Bora is held in one remembered question about prayer. Johann Walter remembered the first German Mass. Paul Speratus is known as the author of three hymns in the first hymn-book. John and Henry, two young monks, were burned at Brussels in 1523 and are known by their first names alone.

documented_stories.teaser: A friar wrote to the archbishop whose name sold the indulgences. He asked for correction. The famous door and hammer come from a later editor, and his letter never mentions them.
documented_stories.text:
On the last day of October, 1517, a friar of the Augustinian order named Martin Luther, who taught theology at the young university in Wittenberg, sat down to write to a man very far above him in rank: Albrecht, Archbishop of Magdeburg and Mainz, Primate of the German church. He addressed him with every mark of deference the age required - "Most Reverend Father in Christ and Most Illustrious Prince" - and named himself, in the same breath, "the dregs of humanity," astonished at his own boldness in writing at all.
The reason he gave was plain. Indulgences for the building of St. Peter's in Rome were being preached under the Archbishop's own name, and Luther did not attack the preaching itself, which he said he had not heard - he grieved instead over what the people who heard it now believed. They believed, he wrote, that a letter of indulgence made their salvation sure the moment it was purchased; that souls flew out of purgatory the instant a coin struck the bottom of the collection box; that no sin was too great to be absolved this way, "even, as they say - though the thing is impossible - if one had violated the Mother of God"; and that the letters freed a person from guilt as well as penalty. "O God, most good!" he wrote. "Thus souls committed to your care, good Father, are taught to their death." He asked the Archbishop, as a father would be asked, to look at the matter and withdraw the instruction the preachers were working from, before someone else did it in public and to the Archbishop's own shame. He closed asking the Lord to keep "your Most Reverend Fatherhood eternally," signed himself simply "Brother Martin Luther," and added one line more: if it pleased the Most Reverend Father, he might look over "these my Disputations" - the ninety-five statements Luther had drawn up for university debate, sent along with the letter, on how doubtful a thing the preachers' confidence about indulgences really was.
That is the act this library can show directly, dated and in Luther's own hand: a formal protest, addressed upward through the church's own channels, to a superior, asking for correction rather than announcing a break. What happened to the Theses after that - whether they were also nailed, that same day or another, to the door of Wittenberg's Castle Church, the way announcements for university debate were customarily posted - is a separate and much less certain question. The account of a door and a hammer that many people know today comes from a much later editor's own narrative telling, not from Luther's own words, and modern scholars have disputed whether it happened at all. The letter to Albrecht is not in question. The door is.
documented_stories.title: A Letter to an Archbishop

documented_stories.teaser: Luther came back from hiding without his prince's leave. He found the city in disorder and told his own congregation they had learned the words of reform and not yet its love.
documented_stories.text:
In March of 1522, Luther left the Wartburg - the fortress where he had been sheltered, against his own will, after Worms - and rode back to Wittenberg without the Elector's leave. The reform he had set moving had begun to run ahead of him in his absence, under the leadership of his own colleague Karlstadt, and Wittenberg, by the account this library holds, had fallen into disorder over exactly how fast the old forms of worship should be swept away.
Luther preached eight days running on his return, and the first of those sermons survives in this library, though not from its very beginning - a witness named Kessler, who was present, recalled afterward that Luther set aside his prepared opening and spoke directly to "the present affair" instead, and the printed text as this library holds it begins already inside that address.
What Luther told his own congregation, in that sermon, was not gentle. "And here, dear friends," he said, "have you not grievously failed? I see no signs of love among you." He told them plainly that learning the doctrine was not the same as living it: "Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum... an ass can almost intone the lessons, and why should you not be able to repeat the doctrines and formulas?" The kingdom of God, he said, "consists not in speech or in words, but in deeds, in works and exercises. God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers who exercise themselves in the faith that worketh by love." A faith without love, he told them, was not faith at all - "a counterfeit of faith."
That sermon, and the seven that followed it across the same week, are this library's clearest single instance of Luther restraining his own movement's fastest wing rather than driving it forward - returning, uninvited, to slow down a change he himself had set in motion.
documented_stories.title: Eight Days of Preaching

documented_stories.teaser: Melanchthon wrote it, and it was read before the Emperor. An elector, princes, and two city senates signed. In this record, Luther did not sign.
documented_stories.text:
In 1530, the Emperor summoned a Diet of the Empire to Augsburg - called, by the confession's own preface, to deliberate "concerning measures against the Turk, that most atrocious, hereditary, and ancient enemy of the Christian name and religion," and, alongside that, to hear out the religious divisions splitting the German lands. Before that assembly, a confession of the movement's own teaching was read and presented: drafted by Melanchthon, addressed directly to "Most Invincible Emperor, Caesar Augustus, Most Clement Lord."
What makes this document unlike every other story in this library is who stands behind it. It is not signed by Luther, and it does not speak in one man's voice. It closes with a list of names: John, Duke of Saxony and Elector; George, Margrave of Brandenburg; Ernest, Duke of Lueneburg; Philip, Landgrave of Hesse; John Frederick, Duke of Saxony; Francis, Duke of Lueneburg; Wolfgang, Prince of Anhalt; and the Senate and Magistracy of Nuremberg and of Reutlingen among the free cities - princes and city councils together, naming themselves before the Emperor as "your Imperial Majesty's faithful subjects."
This is the movement's own act of confessional self-definition, made not as a protest but as a formal, corporate act of loyal address - the same posture, at institutional scale, that Luther's own letter to Albrecht had opened in 1517: correction offered upward, through the proper channel, rather than a break announced from outside it.
documented_stories.title: A Confession Signed by Princes

floor_note.text: On who Jesus is, this world gives the answer its households said each week. Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. It treats this as received teaching that its own history never had to settle. What it stresses is what he did. He bought back lost people at the cost of his own blood, and he alone stands as their Mediator. Faith in him is trust in a promise.

legacy.text: This world's own record says that a confessional family grew from these churches. It still teaches a catechism like this world's own and still sings in the language of the people, under many names. This record speaks from the world's own formation, as it was lived. It makes no claim about what those communities believe or practice now.

Three things are not carried forward. This record does not say what came after the prince-and-council church that this world lived under. It closes within a few years of the founder's death, though the confession it holds was gathered by 1580. The tradition went on for centuries beyond that point, in ways not told here. The 1543 treatise is real and part of this world's own history. This record does not say how the churches that came after have answered for it.

read_first.note: The household program in the founder's own words: the three parts, the weekly questions, and the scripts for confession. This edition lacks Luther's 1529 preface. It describes what a household was to do and holds nothing of what any household did.

The founder's own account of why the catechism was needed. It sets out the father's weekly duty to examine his household. His complaint that people held the Gospel lightly is his own word, and no parish report backs it.
This world's own statement of its teaching, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530 by an elector, princes, and two city senates. It speaks as a shared voice.

relations_summary.text: This world knew itself partly by what it refused. It refused the claim that authority over doctrine sits with the pope, and it refused the sale of indulgences. Rome answered with a bull in 1520 and a written reply at Augsburg in 1530. It also set limits against the radicals of 1522, and its confession names and condemns the Anabaptists. And it broke with the cities that read the Supper differently, at Marburg in 1529. The Roman side reaches this record only as quoted by the side that answered it.

sourcing.text: This record is richest in the founder's catechisms, treatises, and confessional documents. It is also rich in the movement's own account of its founding decade, 1517 to 1531. It is thinner elsewhere. No parish's own report of receiving this teaching is held. The Saxon visitation records exist but are not in this library. No woman's own text is in this library. The felt experience of the 1529 break at Marburg has not come down to this record. The years after 1531, up to the declared close of 1580, are thin. This library holds no object or outside witness that confirms this world's account of itself. Two real parts of its history are not available to quote: the 1525 tract against the peasants and the 1543 treatise against the Jews.

story.text: This world runs from 1517 to 1580. It opens with theses against the sale of indulgences, written in 1517. It closes with a fuller book of confessions, gathered in 1580 from documents written decades before. The record runs deepest to about 1531 and thins sharply after that. The founder's life ended in the mid-1540s, and the years after reach us only through the 1580 book. This record does not describe those years as if it had lived them.

On 31 October 1517, a friar named Martin Luther wrote to Albrecht, the Archbishop of Mainz. Luther taught theology at the young university in Wittenberg. Indulgences for building St. Peter's in Rome were being preached under the archbishop's name. Luther grieved over what people now believed. He asked the archbishop to withdraw the preachers' instructions. He sent ninety-five statements with it, to be debated. The letter asks for correction. It says nothing of a hammer or a church door. That scene comes from a much later editor, and scholars dispute it.

Rome pressed him to take his words back. Years later, at his own table, Luther told students about Augsburg in 1518. Before the papal legate, Cardinal Cajetan, he was urged to say one word: Revoco, I recant. A bull of June 1520 condemned forty-one of his statements. In 1521 he stood before the Emperor and the princes at Worms. By his own later account, he said he could not give up his teaching, though he was willing to be corrected on his harsher polemics. The famous sentence about taking his stand at Worms is absent from his own account as this record holds it, and scholars dispute its authenticity.

The reform soon ran ahead of its founder. In March 1522, Luther left the Wartburg without his prince's leave and rode back to Wittenberg. His colleague Karlstadt had led a fast change in worship, and the city was in disorder. Luther preached eight days in a row. He told his congregation they had gone too fast and that he saw little love among them. He told them a faith without love was not faith at all. He taught that what is free should never be made compulsory. By 1529 he turned the word liberty against pastors grown careless. The record keeps both uses.

The reform's chief tool was the household catechism of 1529. It has three parts: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer. A household was to say them at rising, at table, and at night. A father was to question his children and servants at least once a week. A child who could not say the words was to get no food or drink until he could. After each part came one question: what does this mean? Servants and masters each had their own words for confession. This is the program as written, and the record does not show any household keeping it.

The commandments, as this world read them, show a person what he cannot do. A terrified conscience then has nowhere to rest. The promises of God stand ready: a sinner is freely made right for Christ's sake, through faith. The sacraments carry that promise. Baptism is daily, and absolution is given as though from God himself. At the Supper, the promise is spoken to each person who receives. The Mass was kept, and none came to the Supper without being examined. This world holds that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, and it gives no explanation of how.

German hymns were sung inside the Mass to teach the people. Latin stayed for those learning it. Johann Walter remembered, some forty years later, being kept three weeks at Wittenberg. He and Luther chose how to sing the Epistle and Gospel in German during that time. Wittenberg's first hymn-book came out in 1524. It held four hymns, and Paul Speratus wrote three of them. A tradition says a wanderer from Prussia once sang one under Luther's window. The record holds it only as tradition, and it neither names the singer nor says the singer was Speratus.

On 1 July 1523, two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels. Theologians from Louvain had pressed them to give up what they now taught. They refused. Within months, Luther wrote a ballad about them. It is the only martyr-song in this record. It is also the only case in this record where the movement's teaching cost lives. The ballad says that, stripped of their habits and their ordination, they became true priests of God's own making. Its details, such as their last words, are the ballad's own telling, and no other source confirms them. The record gives no family names or ages for either man.

In 1530 the Emperor called the Diet of Augsburg to plan a defense against the Turk and to hear the religious divisions. A confession of this world's teaching, drafted by Melanchthon, was read and signed. Luther is not among the nine signers in this record. They were an elector, princes, and the senates of two free cities. The document is closer to a treaty than a manifesto, and it takes the form of a loyal address. Rome's theologians answered it in writing. This world replied in a second document, the Apology.

This world broke plainly with the cities that read the Lord's Supper differently. The break came at Marburg in 1529. This world held that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, and it rejected those who teach otherwise. The record holds that position and the fact of the break but not the argument. The Marburg Articles of October 1529 are known, but this library does not have them. The name Zwingli does not appear in the texts searched. What the break felt like from this side has not come down to this record.

Two real parts of this world's history are not available to quote. In 1525, Luther wrote against the peasants' rising. In 1543, he wrote a treatise against the Jews. Both are part of this history, and neither is denied. The record holds only that each exists. It holds neither text, and it does not lay out their arguments. Scholars disagree about the treatise's effect in later centuries. This record cannot settle that, because it has read neither side.

The record is quietest on how people lived all this. The Saxon church inspected its parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist, but this record does not hold them. Luther said more than once that common people took the Gospel too lightly. This is his own testimony, and no parish report in this record confirms it. No woman's own text survives in this library. This record holds one question of Katharina von Bora's, remembered by a student. No outsider's own account of this world is held here either. Rome's reply reaches us only as quoted and answered in this world's own Apology.

dates.display: Directly attested in this library's own sources from 31 October 1517 (the letter to Albrecht) to 9 June 1532 (the prayer for rain); no vendored primary text held here gives a birth date. His life is understood to run into 1546, per this world's own already-established closing boundary - a boundary this record treats as given, not independently re-derived from any source of its own.

names.name: Doctor Martin Luther
Martin Luther (letter dated 1517; no birth or death date attested in this library)

voices.hedge: Many stories of Luther here come from students' notes, written down later. The record gives no birth date, no description, and no biography before 1517. His complaints about careless parishes come from him alone. No report from any actual parish backs them.
voices.text: Luther was the friar and Wittenberg professor who wrote to Archbishop Albrecht about indulgences in 1517. He later told his students of facing a papal legate in 1518 and the Empire's assembly at Worms in 1521. In 1522 he came home to calm his own congregation. This record holds him in his own letters, sermons, catechisms, and a ballad. It also holds table talk that students collected. His life closed in the mid-1540s.

dates.display: Documented in this library only as the Augsburg Confession's own drafter, 1530; no vendored source held here gives any other date for him.

names.name: Melanchthon
Philip Melanchthon, drafter of the Augsburg Confession (1530)

voices.hedge: This record knows Melanchthon only as the Confession's drafter. It holds no biography, no private letter, and no word of his outside the Confession's shared voice. The record presents the story as a signed act of many people.
voices.text: Melanchthon wrote the Augsburg Confession. It was read to the Emperor in 1530, and princes and city senates signed it. It was a shared statement of what the movement taught.

dates.display: Undated in this library beyond the general span of Luther's own household life as Table Talk records it (a collection compiled mainly in the 1530s-40s, per its own transmission history); no vendored source held here gives her birth or death date, or a date for the one exchange this library records.

names.name: Kate, Luther's wife
Katharina von Bora

voices.hedge: That question is the only place any woman speaks in this record. It passed through several hands, and its exact wording is Contested. This record holds nothing else of her words, her days, or her convictions. It can carry no more than one sentence.
voices.text: Katharina von Bora was Luther's wife. One question of hers survives in this record. She asked why the old church prayed with such fervor while their own household prayed so coldly. A student remembered it and wrote it down years later.

dates.display: Undated in this library beyond his own letter's self-description, written "in his old age," recalling events "some forty years" past; the German Mass work he describes belongs to the mid-1520s (Luther's own effort to establish it), per his own account as quoted in Bacon's Introduction.

names.name: Johann Walter, Luther's musical collaborator
Johann Walter (letter written "in his old age," recalling events of some forty years earlier)

voices.hedge: Walter wrote in his old age, about events some forty years back. His letter reaches this record only as quoted by a later editor, through three earlier hands. It praises Luther throughout, and no second witness confirms it.
voices.text: Johann Walter worked with Luther on the music. He remembered being kept three weeks at Wittenberg while the two of them chose how to sing the Epistle and Gospel in German. His letter is the one account of worship there that does not come from Luther himself.

tile.text: In 1517, Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at the young university of Wittenberg, wrote to his archbishop against the sale of indulgences. The letter began a movement that set Scripture against a hierarchy standing between people and God. It held that a person stands before God by a gift received through faith, apart from works. Princes and city councils took the reform into their lands in place of bishops. This world's chief tool was the household catechism. It had three parts, to be said at rising, at table, and at night. A father or a schoolmaster was to examine each household every week. The commandments left the conscience afraid, and a promise spoken from outside it made the conscience sure. German hymns were sung inside a Mass that was kept. The story runs from the Ninety-Five Theses to a confession signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530. It closes with a fuller book of confessions, gathered in 1580. The record is rich on the founding decade. It is thin on how any household or parish lived this, and this library holds no woman's own text.
